manuscript_locations.anchor: Loss from penalty selection exceeds half
manuscript_locations.excerpt: Loss from penalty selection exceeds half of positive actual excess loss in 27 of 41 short-history weekly comparisons (Figure~\ref{fig:v12-decomposition}). Extending validation lowers CFTC median excess loss from 19.33\% to 4.03\% with short histories, and from 10.35\% to 0.53\% with longer histories. The New York Fed medians fall from 6.68\% to -1.13\% at horizon six and from 40.47\% to 5.02\% at horizon twenty-four (Table~\ref{tab:v13-validation}). Yet the best finite penalty selected with evaluation hindsight still loses to historical headroom in 29 of 41 comparisons. This residual gap indicates limited incremental information within the tested feature set and finite menu.

manuscript_locations.anchor: both long-history FX horizons have negative finite-menu gaps
manuscript_locations.excerpt: The decomposition separates the selected report's gap from the best finite candidate and that candidate's gap from historical headroom. The retrospective finite candidate uses five penalties and excludes the ordinary empirical limit, supplying a diagnostic rather than a deployable selection rule. Separate component medians need not add: actual excess is 19.44\%, selection 18.32\%, and the diagnostic gap 4.37\%. An empirical-limit selection can beat every finite candidate, making its selection component negative; both long-history FX horizons have negative finite-menu gaps.

manuscript_locations.anchor: 8 cases lose by over ten percent
manuscript_locations.excerpt: The protocol combines the six-point menu in Table~\ref{tab:methods}, longer validation and a corrected-rank historical default. It selects the lowest mean validation loss over 156 weekly observations or 5,760 FX records. The selected candidate replaces historical headroom only when its paired validation improvement strictly exceeds one HAC standard error \citep{nw1987}. Across 60 weekly comparisons, the protocol retains historical headroom in 32 and has 0.00\% median excess, compared with 14.63\% for ordinary regression. This zero median reflects the majority of decisions retaining historical headroom. However, 8 cases lose by over ten percent, exceeding the prewritten five-percent ceiling for such cases; the worst excess is 80.98\% (Figure~\ref{fig:v13-rp}). Both FX periods retain the ordinary regression gains, meeting the criterion for retaining gains. The rule was designed after earlier findings and uses inspected evaluation periods, so this check is retrospective.

manuscript_locations.anchor: The median condition therefore passes while the tail condition fails
manuscript_locations.excerpt: All 62 planned comparisons complete, including 60 weekly cells and both FX periods. The weekly median moves from +14.63\% for ordinary regression with the six-point menu to 0.00\% for the protocol. However, 8 of 60 weekly cells exceed the historical loss by more than 10\%, and the worst excess is +80.98\%. The median condition therefore passes while the tail condition fails. The protocol returns to history in 32 weekly cells and uses regression in 28, as Table~\ref{tab:v13-routing} shows. The adverse cells comprise 7 CFTC comparisons and 1 New York Fed comparison. Both FX periods retain their ordinary-regression gains, 14.77\% and 16.62\%, meeting the gain-retention condition.
